analysis.one_liner: Opens part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil and gas drilling with strict environmental conditions.
analysis.headline: The Senate Energy Committee held hearings and wrote a replacement bill, but neither version ever came to a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have opened about 1.5 million acres of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's Coastal Plain to competitive oil and gas leasing, capped at 300,000 acres per sale. It paired that with unusually strict conditions: a 'no significant adverse effect' standard for wildlife, performance bonds, strict liability for oil spills, and a reclamation fund paid for by a fee on oil entering the trans-Alaska pipeline. Lease revenue would have been split, with half going to Alaska and 40% to federal conservation funds. The Senate Energy Committee held hearings and marked the bill up, then wrote its own bill (S. 684) to take its place — and neither version ever reached the Senate floor.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain the right to bid on leases across the Coastal Plain of the Arctic Refuge, one of the largest prospective onshore oil areas under federal control. The State of Alaska would receive 50% of all lease and royalty revenue, and Inupiat Eskimo subsurface owners would have federal limits on developing their subsurface interests repealed.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies and the State of Alaska

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes and directs the Interior Secretary to run a competitive oil and gas leasing program on the roughly 1.549-million-acre Coastal Plain of the Arctic Refuge, with lease sales of up to 300,000 acres each.
Grants leases to the highest qualified bidder with a royalty of at least 12.5% of production, and requires the public to receive fair market value for the minerals.
Splits leasing revenue 50% to the State of Alaska, 25% to the Land and Water Conservation Fund, 15% to wetland protection and restoration, and 10% to the Treasury.

Repeals federal limits under the 1980 Alaska lands act on the subsurface oil and gas interests owned by the Inupiat Eskimo people within and adjacent to the Coastal Plain, subject to the bill's environmental rules.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost of industrial development inside a national wildlife refuge: risks to caribou, birds, and other wildlife and their habitat, to the area's subsistence users, and to the environment from spills — backed by a cleanup fund capped at $50 million, far below the cost of a major spill. The one-time revenue is a drawdown of a publicly owned resource that, once leased, cannot be unleased.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and the Arctic refuge

drawbacks.text: The bill's own reclamation fund stops collecting once it holds $50 million, an amount that would cover only a small fraction of the damage from a major oil spill in the Arctic; a spill there is exceptionally hard to clean up.

The bill's central promise — that drilling will cause 'no significant adverse effect on fish and wildlife, their habitat, and the environment' — depends on Interior Department regulations and enforcement that the bill itself cannot guarantee, and it authorizes rights-of-way for pipelines and roads across the refuge.

Once the refuge's Coastal Plain is leased, surface disturbance follows as a matter of course; the bill designates the 4,000-acre Sadlerochit Spring area for protection but allows the Secretary to lease even that area as long as there is no surface occupancy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a deliberate compromise: it opened the refuge to drilling but with stricter conditions than most leasing proposals — strict liability for pollution, twice-yearly facility inspections, a reclamation standard restoring land to its original condition, and revenue for conservation. Even so, the fundamental trade stays the same: a permanently altered wildlife refuge and spill risk in one of the country's most fragile environments, exchanged for royalty revenue and oil supply. The $50 million cleanup fund is the weakest link — it would not come close to covering a catastrophe, leaving taxpayers exposed to the excess.

outcome.mechanism: After hearings and two markup sessions, the Senate Energy Committee voted to report its own bill (S. 684) in place of this one, and neither version ever came up for a vote on the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. J. Bennett Johnston introduced the bill on February 9, 1989, joined by Sen. McClure; it was read twice and referred to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
The committee requested comments from Interior and the budget office, held hearings on March 6, 1989, and held markup sessions on March 8 and March 15.
On March 16, 1989, the committee ordered favorably reported an original bill, S. 684, in lieu of S. 406 — meaning it wrote a separate bill to take this one's place.
The committee held additional hearings in July, August, and November 1989, including a field hearing in Baton Rouge, Louisiana.
No further action was recorded: the bill, and the substitute bill, never received a vote by the full Senate, and the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies gained no access to the refuge this Congress, and the Arctic Refuge's Coastal Plain remained closed to leasing — so those who wanted the refuge protected were better off than they would have been had the bill passed.

for.name: Sen. J. Bennett Johnston
for.role: Senator from Louisiana; Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, referred it to the committee he chaired, which held hearings, marked it up, and reported a substitute bill in its place.

for.name: Sen. McClure
for.what_they_did: Joined Johnston in introducing the bill; two Republicans cosponsored it in total.

against.name: Environmental and conservation organizations
against.role: National groups opposing drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
against.what_they_did: Opposed opening the refuge to oil and gas leasing, keeping the issue contentious enough that the Senate never brought a drilling bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: A Democrat sponsored the bill with two Republican cosponsors, and no votes were ever recorded, so the partisan split is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have opened the Arctic Refuge's Coastal Plain to competitive leasing, giving companies access to one of the largest untapped onshore oil areas in the United States. The industry's gain comes from developing a publicly owned wildlife refuge, with spill and habitat risks borne by the public.

The bill would have made the pipeline's right-of-way holder the administrator of a new Coastal Plain cleanup and reclamation fund, collecting a five-cent-per-barrel fee on refuge oil entering the pipeline — a permanent new role tied to whatever development followed.

The bill would have repealed federal limits on oil and gas development of subsurface interests these Alaska Native owners hold within and adjacent to the Coastal Plain, while applying the same environmental rules to their development.
